result.source_concept: Occupied but Ignored Chair (a chair that is sat in once but never utilized)

mappings.relation: Both serve as a location that can be occupied once
mappings.evidence: The analogy describes a special chair that can only be sat in once, mirroring a variable that is assigned a value exactly once.

mappings.target_element: Assigning a value to the variable
mappings.evidence: "When a student sits in this chair (the variable is assigned a value)"

mappings.relation: Representation of the data held in the location
mappings.evidence: "they write their name on a clipboard (the value is stored)"

mappings.source_element: Nobody checking the clipboard or calling on the student
mappings.relation: Lack of subsequent access to the stored data
mappings.evidence: "if nobody ever calls on that student or checks the clipboard ... the variable is never read or used"

mappings.source_element: Teacher placing a sticky note warning on the chair
mappings.target_element: Compiler or linter issuing a warning about the singleton variable
mappings.relation: Observer detecting wasteful occupancy and signaling a warning
mappings.evidence: "teacher (compiler or linter) notices this inefficiency and puts a yellow sticky note on the chair as a warning"

mappings.source_element: Unused chair taking up space in the classroom
mappings.target_element: Singleton variable occupying memory without functional benefit
mappings.evidence: "Just like that unused chair takes up space ... a singleton variable occupies memory ... without contributing to its functionality"

result.process_summary: In both the chair scenario and the singleton variable case, an entity is occupied/assigned once, stores a piece of information, but is never accessed again. An external observer (teacher or compiler/linter) detects this inefficiency and issues a warning, highlighting that the occupied resource consumes space without providing benefit.
potential_breaks: A physical chair can be removed without affecting the classroom, whereas removing a variable may require code changes; the analogy glosses over this difference.
